title: CSS Fundamentals
description: Learn how CSS works under the hood. Master selectors, specificity, the cascade, inheritance, and the box model — the four pillars that underpin every CSS decision you will ever make.
learningObjectives: Write CSS using element, class, id, attribute, and pseudo selectors
Understand how specificity determines which rule wins
Master the box model: content, padding, border, margin
Use display, position, and overflow properties

sections.content: Targeting Elements with Selectors
A CSS rule has two parts: a selector (what to target) and a declaration block (what to apply). Selectors range from simple element names to powerful combinators and pseudo-classes.

exercises.question: Which selector targets only direct children of .nav, not deeper descendants?
exercises.explanation: .nav > li selects li elements that are direct children of .nav. .nav li would also match deeply nested li elements.

sections.content: The Cascade — How Conflicts Are Resolved

When multiple rules target the same element with the same property, the cascade resolves the conflict using three factors in order: 1) Origin (author vs browser default), 2) Specificity (how specific the selector is), 3) Source order (last rule wins if equal specificity).
Specificity Scoring
Specificity is calculated as a three-part score: (IDs, Classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, Elements/pseudo-elements). Higher scores win.
⚠️ Avoid !important — it breaks the cascade and creates tech debt. Instead, increase selector specificity or restructure your CSS.

exercises.question: Given these rules for the same element, which color wins? 1) p { color: red; } 2) .intro { color: blue; } 3) #hero p { color: green; }
hints: ID selectors have the highest specificity
exercises.explanation: #hero p has specificity (1,0,1) — one ID and one element. .intro has (0,1,0) and p has (0,0,1). The ID selector wins.

sections.content: Every Element is a Box
The CSS box model defines how every element's total size is calculated. From inside out: content → padding → border → margin. Understanding this is foundational to all layout work.
🎯 Always add * { box-sizing: border-box; } at the top of every CSS file. It makes width/height behave intuitively.

exercises.question: With box-sizing: content-box, what is the total rendered width of an element with width:200px, padding:20px, border:5px?
exercises.explanation: content-box: total = 200 + 20+20 + 5+5 = 250px. With border-box, total would be 200px (padding/border eat into the content area).

The position Property

exercises.question: You want a navbar that stays at the top of the screen as the user scrolls. Which position value should you use?
hints: It should not move at all during scroll
exercises.explanation: position: fixed removes the element from document flow and positions it relative to the viewport — it won't move when the page scrolls.

sections.content: CSS Custom Properties (Variables)

CSS custom properties (variables) store reusable values. Defined with -- prefix, accessed with var(). They are scoped, inheritable, and can be changed at runtime with JavaScript — unlike Sass variables.
CSS Reset / Normalise

exercises.question: What is the correct way to access a CSS custom property named --brand-color?
hints: Custom properties use a special function to read their values
exercises.explanation: CSS custom properties are accessed using the var() function. The -- prefix is required both when declaring and referencing them.

capstoneProject.title: Styled Component Library
capstoneProject.description: Build a mini design system: define CSS variables, write a reset, and create 5 reusable components (button, card, badge, input, alert) styled purely with the concepts from this module.
requirements: :root block with at least 8 CSS variables (colors, spacing, radii, font)
Modern CSS reset at the top of the file
Input with :focus ring matching WCAG contrast
